This we shall use as the left-hand side of Eq. (7.33). For the right-hand side,
we need an estimate for _θ_ ( _x_ ) in terms of _δ_ ( _x_ ). If we use the logarithmic law
profile (7.34), we shall be up to our hips in logarithmic integrations for the
momentum thickness. Instead we follow another suggestion of Prandtl, who
pointed out that the turbulent profiles in Fig. 7.5 can be approximated by a oneseventh-power law:

This is shown as a dashed line in Fig. 7.5. It is an excellent fit to the lowReynolds-number turbulent data, which were all that were available to Prandtl at
the time. With this simple approximation, the momentum thickness (7.28) can
easily be evaluated:

We accept this result and substitute Eqs. (7.38) and (7.40) into Kármán’s
momentum law (7.33):

Separate the variables and integrate, assuming _δ_ = 0 at _x_ = 0:

Thus the thickness of a turbulent boundary layer increases as _x_ <sup>6/7</sup>, far more
rapidly than the laminar increase _x_ <sup>1/2</sup> . Equation (7.42) is the solution to the
problem, because all other parameters are now available. For example,
combining Eqs. (7.42) and (7.38), we obtain the friction variation

Writing this out in dimensional form, we have

Turbulent plate friction drops slowly with _x_, increases nearly as _ρ_ and _U_ <sup>2</sup>,
and is rather insensitive to viscosity.

We can evaluate the drag coefficient by integrating the wall friction:

Then _CD_ is only 16 percent greater than the trailing-edge skin friction
coefficient [compare with Eq. (7.27) for laminar flow].

The displacement thickness can be estimated from the one-seventh-power
law and Eq. (7.12):

The turbulent flat-plate shape factor is approximately

These are the basic results of turbulent flat-plate theory.

Figure 7.6 shows flat-plate drag coefficients for both laminar and turbulent
flow conditions. The smooth-wall relations (7.27) and (7.45) are shown, along
with the effect of wall roughness, which is quite strong. The proper roughness

parameter here is _x_ / _ϵ_ or _L_ / _ϵ_, by analogy with the pipe parameter _ϵ_ / _d_ . In the fully
rough regime, _CD_ is independent of the Reynolds number, so that the drag varies
exactly as _U_ <sup>2</sup> and is independent of _μ_ . Reference 2 presents a theory of rough
flat-plate flow, and Ref. 1 gives a curve fit for skin friction and drag in the fully
rough regime:

figure also shows the behavior of the drag coefficient in the transition region 5 ×
